breakfast.name: Jok (Rice Congee)
ingredients: Spring onion, coriander, crispy garlic (to garnish)
instructions: Jok is the Thai rice porridge -- the Thai comfort breakfast
Jasmine rice cooked in a large amount of water or broth until completely broken down and silky
The ratio: about 1:10 rice to liquid -- far more liquid than regular rice
Stirred constantly as it thickens
The meat is added as small balls that poach in the congee
Ginger and white pepper are the signature flavors
Garnished with spring onion, coriander, fried garlic, and often a soft-boiled egg
Sold at street stalls from dawn -- Thais eat it any time of day
breakfast.description: Thai rice porridge -- jasmine rice cooked in a large volume of broth (1:10 ratio) until silky and broken down. Ginger and white pepper are the signature flavors. Pork or chicken balls poach in the congee. Garnished with fried garlic, spring onion, and a soft-boiled egg. Sold at street stalls from dawn.

breakfast.name: Khao Tom (Rice Soup)
instructions: Khao tom is the Thai clear rice soup -- different from jok (congee)
Where jok uses uncooked rice cooked down to a porridge, khao tom uses already-cooked rice in a clear broth
The broth is light and savory -- fish sauce and white pepper
The rice stays separate in the soup, not broken down
Lighter than jok -- popular for those who want a more delicate breakfast
breakfast.description: Thai clear rice soup -- cooked jasmine rice in a light chicken broth with ginger and fish sauce. Unlike jok (congee), the rice stays intact and the broth remains clear. Lighter and more delicate than porridge. Often eaten when unwell or for a gentle start to the day.

breakfast.name: Kai Jeow (Thai Omelette)
ingredients: Oil (for deep frying -- a generous amount)
instructions: Kai jeow is the Thai omelette -- a street food staple eaten over rice
The Thai omelette is different from French: it is puffed and crispy
The eggs are beaten with fish sauce and white pepper
Fried in a generous amount of hot oil -- the egg puffs up dramatically
The outside is crispy and slightly caramelized
The inside remains soft
Placed on top of white rice -- the rice soaks up the oil and egg flavor
Fish sauce replaces salt -- the key Thai seasoning
breakfast.description: Thai puffed omelette over rice -- eggs beaten with fish sauce and white pepper, fried in generous hot oil until dramatically puffed and crispy outside, soft inside. Placed over jasmine rice that soaks up the flavored oil. Fish sauce is the Thai salt. A street-food staple eaten at any hour.

breakfast.name: Pad Kra Pao Kai Dow (Holy Basil Stir-Fry with Fried Egg)
ingredients: Thai holy basil (kra pao -- NOT sweet basil)
Fish sauce, oyster sauce, dark soy sauce
instructions: Pad kra pao is one of the most popular Thai dishes -- the national comfort food
Thai holy basil (kra pao) is distinct from Italian and sweet basil -- more peppery, anise-like, and wilts dramatically when cooked
The stir-fry is extremely aromatic: garlic and bird's eye chilli fried in hot oil first
The pork or chicken goes in and is cooked over very high heat
The holy basil is added at the last moment -- it wilts quickly and the heat releases its oils
Always served with a crispy fried egg on top (kai dao -- star egg) with runny yolk
The yolk breaks over the spicy meat -- the cooling richness against the heat
Available at every Thai rice shop (khao rad gaeng stall) and late at night
breakfast.description: Thai holy basil stir-fry -- pork or chicken stir-fried over screaming heat with garlic, bird's eye chilli, and Thai holy basil (kra pao: peppery, anise-forward, different from sweet basil). Topped with a crispy fried egg (kai dao). The yolk breaks over the spicy meat. Served over jasmine rice at every Thai rice shop and midnight stall.

lunch.name: Pad Thai (Stir-Fried Rice Noodles)
ingredients: Thin rice noodles (sen lek -- soaked in cold water)
Tamarind paste, fish sauce, palm sugar
Roasted peanuts, lime, dried chilli flakes (for garnish)
instructions: Pad Thai is the most internationally known Thai dish -- but the Thai version differs from overseas versions
The flavor is balanced: sour from tamarind, salty from fish sauce, sweet from palm sugar
The noodles (sen lek) are soaked, not boiled, before stir-frying -- they stay slightly al dente
Dried shrimp give an umami base that is often omitted overseas
The egg is scrambled directly in the wok with the noodles
Bean sprouts are added at the last moment for crunch -- they must not overcook
Served with condiments: roasted peanuts, lime, dried chilli, fish sauce
The diner seasons it to taste -- each person's pad thai is different
Pad Thai was promoted by the Thai government in the 1940s (Plaek Phibunsongkhram) to create a national identity dish and reduce rice consumption during shortage
lunch.description: Thai stir-fried rice noodles -- sen lek noodles stir-fried with shrimp, egg, dried shrimp, and tamarind-fish sauce-palm sugar balance. Bean sprouts for crunch, roasted peanuts and lime to finish. The diner seasons to taste. Promoted as a national dish by the Thai government in the 1940s to create national identity.

lunch.name: Tom Yum Goong (Spicy Sour Shrimp Soup)
ingredients: Nam prik pao (roasted chilli paste -- for the creamy version)
Evaporated milk (for tom yum nam khon -- the rich version)
instructions: Tom yum is one of Thailand's most famous soups -- an intense, sour, spicy, fragrant broth
The three key aromatics: lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves
These are bruised and simmered -- they flavor the broth but are not eaten
The shrimp is cooked in the broth -- it poaches quickly
Nam pla (fish sauce) and lime: the salt and acid
Tom yum nam sai: the clear version -- lighter, more acidic
Tom yum nam khon: the creamy version -- nam prik pao and evaporated milk added
The creamy version is the most popular internationally
The lemongrass, galangal, and kaffir lime: the trinity of Thai sour soups
lunch.description: Thai spicy-sour shrimp soup -- shrimp poached in a broth built on the trinity of lemongrass, galangal, and kaffir lime leaves. Two versions: clear (nam sai, acidic) and creamy (nam khon, with roasted chilli paste and evaporated milk). Fish sauce and lime are the salt and acid. The aromatics flavor the broth; they are not eaten.

lunch.name: Som Tam (Green Papaya Salad)
ingredients: Fish sauce, lime juice, palm sugar
Optional: salted crab (poo dong) for the Isan version
instructions: Som tam is the northeastern Thai (Isan) salad that has become Thailand's most popular dish
Made in a clay mortar -- the pestle pounds the aromatics, then the ingredients are bruised (not crushed)
The technique: pound the garlic and chilli first, then add the other ingredients and toss-pound
The green papaya provides crunch; the tomatoes burst when pounded
The flavor balance: sour (lime), salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), spicy (chilli)
Som tam Thai: with dried shrimp and peanuts (the tourist version)
Som tam poo: with salted fermented crab -- the original Isan version, funkier
Eaten with sticky rice (khao niao) -- the Isan staple
The sound of the mortar: the sonic signature of Thai markets
lunch.description: Thai green papaya salad -- shredded unripe papaya pounded in a clay mortar with garlic, chilli, tomatoes, and long beans, dressed with fish sauce, lime, and palm sugar. Isan origin (northeastern Thailand). Two versions: som tam Thai (dried shrimp, peanuts) and som tam poo (salted fermented crab, the original Isan). Eaten with sticky rice.

lunch.name: Khao Man Gai (Poached Chicken Rice)
ingredients: Jasmine rice (cooked in the chicken fat and broth)
Fermented soybean sauce, ginger, garlic, chilli (for the sauce)
instructions: Khao man gai is the Thai version of Hainanese chicken rice
The Teochew and Hainanese Chinese community brought it to Thailand
The chicken is poached gently until just cooked -- very soft and juicy
The rice is cooked in the chicken fat rendered from poaching and the chicken broth
The rice absorbs all the chicken flavor
The sauce: a pungent mix of fermented soybean sauce, ginger, garlic, chilli, and vinegar
Served with cucumber, coriander, and a separate bowl of clear broth
The Jek (Chinese-Thai) influence: ubiquitous across Bangkok
lunch.description: Thai Chinese-heritage poached chicken rice -- chicken poached until silky-soft, the rendered fat and broth used to cook jasmine rice until fragrant. Served with a pungent fermented soybean-ginger-chilli sauce, cucumber, and clear broth. Brought by Hainanese and Teochew immigrants. Called khao man gai.

lunch.name: Larb (Minced Meat Salad)
ingredients: Minced pork, chicken, or duck (briefly cooked)
Toasted rice powder (khao khua -- dry-toasted then ground)
instructions: Larb is the Isan and Lao dish that is now eaten across Thailand
Minced meat -- cooked briefly (or raw in some versions) -- dressed with lime, fish sauce, and chilli
The essential ingredient: toasted rice powder (khao khua)
Dry toasted until golden, then ground in a mortar -- it thickens the dressing and adds a nutty, toasty flavor
Without khao khua it is not larb
Fresh herbs: shallots, spring onion, coriander, and mint
The mint is the cooling element against the chilli
Eaten with sticky rice
lunch.description: Thai Isan minced meat salad -- pork, chicken, or duck briefly cooked and dressed with lime, fish sauce, chilli, and toasted rice powder (khao khua: dry-toasted rice ground in a mortar, the essential ingredient that thickens and adds nutty toastiness). Fresh mint as the cooling element. Isan origin, shared with Lao cuisine.

dinner.name: Massaman Curry
ingredients: Massaman curry paste (dried chilli, shallots, lemongrass, galangal, coriander, cumin, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, nutmeg -- the Muslim spice influence)
Fish sauce, palm sugar, tamarind paste
instructions: Massaman curry is the southern Thai Muslim curry -- not the mainstream Thai Buddhist cuisine
The name: from Mussalman (Muslim) -- the Muslim influence on southern Thai coastal cuisine
The spice profile is different from all other Thai curries: heavy warm spices
Cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, nutmeg -- these are Indian-Muslim spices, not typical Thai
This reflects the Persian and Indian Muslim trade routes through southern Thailand
The beef is slow-cooked for 1-2 hours until very tender
The curry is mild, rich, slightly sweet, and deeply complex
Massaman was rated the world's best food by CNN Travel in 2011 -- causing a debate about such lists but raising global awareness
dinner.description: Thai southern Muslim slow-cooked curry -- beef braised in coconut milk with massaman paste (warm spices: cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, nutmeg -- Persian-Indian-Muslim trade route influence), potatoes, and peanuts. Mild, rich, sweet, and deeply complex. The most internationally acclaimed Thai curry, reflecting Muslim culinary influence on southern coastal Thai cuisine.

dinner.name: Gaeng Keow Wan (Green Curry)
ingredients: Green curry paste (fresh green chilli, kaffir lime zest, lemongrass, galangal, shrimp paste, coriander root)
Thai eggplant (pea eggplant and green eggplant)
instructions: Green curry (gaeng keow wan) is the most aromatic Thai curry
Made from fresh green chillies -- the color comes from the chillies and herbs
The paste: many fresh ingredients pounded in a mortar for 20-30 minutes by hand
Fried in the coconut cream (the top, thick layer of coconut milk) to release the oils
The sauce: coconut milk added, the curry simmers briefly
Thai eggplant: two types -- pea eggplant (tiny, bitter, pop in the mouth) and the round green eggplant
Thai basil is added at the last moment
Gaeng keow wan: literally green-sweet curry -- the Thai designation
Served with jasmine rice or round rice noodles (khanom jeen)
dinner.description: Thai green curry -- chicken or beef in a sauce of fresh-green-chilli paste fried in coconut cream, thinned with coconut milk. Thai pea eggplant (bitter, pop-in-mouth) and round eggplant. Thai basil at the last moment. Made from fresh green chillies (not dried), the color from the herbs. Gaeng keow wan means green-sweet curry.

dinner.name: Pad See Ew (Stir-Fried Wide Rice Noodles)
ingredients: Wide flat rice noodles (fresh, if possible)
Chinese broccoli (gai lan -- stems and leaves)
Dark soy sauce, light soy sauce
instructions: Pad see ew is the Thai stir-fried wide noodle dish
Chinese (Teochew) origin -- the Jek influence on Thai noodle culture
Wide flat rice noodles (sen yai) are best fresh -- they separate and char beautifully
The high heat of the wok is essential -- the caramelization of the dark soy sauce creates the signature smoky char
This char is called wok hei (the breath of the wok) in Chinese cooking
Chinese broccoli (gai lan) is the traditional vegetable -- the slight bitterness works with the sweet soy
The egg is scrambled directly in the wok with the noodles
dinner.description: Thai stir-fried wide rice noodles -- fresh flat rice noodles charred in a screaming wok with dark soy sauce (the caramelized dark soy creates the wok-hei char), egg, and Chinese broccoli (gai lan). Teochew Chinese origin, embedded in Thai street food culture. The char and dark soy are the dish's identity.

dinner.name: Tom Kha Gai (Coconut Galangal Chicken Soup)
instructions: Tom kha gai is the coconut milk version of tom yum -- rich and aromatic
Tom kha: the soup of galangal (kha = galangal in Thai)
Where tom yum is sour and clear, tom kha is rich from the coconut milk
The galangal is sliced and simmered -- it flavors the broth but is not eaten (too fibrous)
Coconut milk is added: the broth becomes creamy and fragrant
Fish sauce and lime: the final seasoning
The combination of coconut, galangal, lemongrass, and kaffir lime leaves is the quintessential Thai aromatic profile
dinner.description: Thai coconut galangal chicken soup -- chicken poached in coconut milk infused with galangal (kha: the Thai root that names this dish), lemongrass, and kaffir lime leaves. Richer than tom yum from the coconut milk. Fish sauce and lime as the final seasoning. The coconut-galangal-lemongrass-kaffir lime combination is the quintessential Thai aromatic profile.

dinner.name: Khao Niao Mamuang (Mango Sticky Rice)
ingredients: Ripe mango (Thai Carabao mango -- fragrant, honey-sweet)
instructions: Khao niao mamuang is the Thai dessert that has traveled the world
The sticky rice (glutinous rice) is steamed -- it must be soaked overnight first
The coconut sauce: warm coconut milk sweetened and salted -- poured hot over the steamed rice
The rice absorbs the coconut milk completely -- it swells and becomes sticky and rich
The mango: the Carabao mango (mamuang ok rong) is the ideal -- golden, fragrant, honeyed
The season matters: April-June is mango season in Thailand
The warm rice against the cold mango: the temperature contrast is part of the experience
dinner.description: Thai mango sticky rice -- glutinous rice steamed until chewy, soaked in warm sweet-salted coconut milk, served with ripe Carabao mango (Thai honey mango: golden, fragrant). The warm rice and cool mango together are the experience. A seasonal dish: April-June mango season in Thailand. Eaten as dessert or snack from street stalls.

snacks.name: Satay (Grilled Skewers)
ingredients: Satay marinade: turmeric, lemongrass, coriander, cumin, coconut milk, palm sugar
Peanut sauce: peanuts, red curry paste, coconut milk, palm sugar, tamarind
Ajad (cucumber relish): cucumber, shallot, chilli, vinegar, sugar
instructions: Thai satay has roots in the Malay and Indonesian satay tradition
The meat is marinated in a paste fragrant with turmeric and lemongrass
Threaded onto bamboo skewers and grilled over charcoal
Served with peanut sauce and the ajad (cucumber relish)
The ajad is the essential counterpart: the sweetened vinegar cuts the richness of the peanut sauce
Sold at every Thai street market
snacks.description: Thai skewered grilled meat -- chicken or pork marinated in turmeric-lemongrass paste, threaded on bamboo skewers, grilled over charcoal. Served with creamy peanut sauce and ajad (sweet vinegary cucumber relish). Malay-Indonesian origin embedded in Thai street food.

snacks.name: Kanom Buang (Thai Crispy Pancakes)
ingredients: Coconut cream (whipped with egg white and sugar -- the white topping)
Meringue or sweet egg yolk threads (foi thong -- for garnish)
Dried shrimp, pickled radish (for savory version)
instructions: Kanom buang are the Thai crispy street pancakes -- one of the oldest Thai desserts
Extremely thin, crispy shells -- made from a rice flour batter on a special flat iron
Two fillings: sweet (whipped coconut cream and foi thong -- golden egg threads) and savory (dried shrimp, pickled radish)
Made at speed by street vendors -- one motion to spread, one to fill, one to close
The skill is in the thinness of the shell -- it must be paper-thin and immediately crispy
snacks.description: Thai crispy street pancakes -- paper-thin rice flour shells with sweet filling (whipped coconut cream, golden egg threads) or savory filling (dried shrimp, pickled radish). One of the oldest Thai desserts. Made at speed by street vendors: one motion to spread the batter, one to fill, one to close.

snacks.name: Roti (Thai Street Roti)
ingredients: Roti dough (flour, egg, butter, salt, water -- stretched thin)
Banana (for banana roti -- the most popular)
instructions: Thai street roti is the Muslim-origin flatbread now sold at every Thai night market
Brought by Muslim traders from southern Thailand (and originally India and Malaysia)
The roti vendor flips the stretched dough with a dramatic spin
Folded around banana and egg on the griddle
Finished with condensed milk and sugar
Thai roti differs from Indian roti -- it is lighter, thinner, more like a crepe
snacks.description: Thai Muslim-origin street roti -- flour dough stretched thin and spun dramatically, folded around banana and egg on a griddle, finished with condensed milk. Brought by Muslim traders from southern Thailand and the broader Malay world. Lighter and thinner than Indian roti; the vendor's spinning is the show.

snacks.name: Miang Kham (Betel Leaf Bites)
ingredients: Betel leaves (or spinach leaves as substitute)
Palm sugar-fish sauce-lime sauce (sweet and sour)
instructions: Miang kham is the Thai one-bite snack -- each component wrapped in a betel leaf
Everything is assembled: a little roasted coconut, shrimp, peanuts, lime, shallot, ginger, chilli, and the sauce
Wrapped in the betel leaf and eaten in one bite
The explosion of flavors: sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, umami -- all at once
A royal Thai snack with ancient roots
Often served at the beginning of a formal Thai meal
snacks.description: Thai one-bite betel leaf wrap -- roasted coconut, dried shrimp, peanuts, lime, shallot, ginger, and chilli assembled on a betel leaf with palm sugar-fish sauce sauce, eaten in a single bite. Sweet-sour-salty-spicy-bitter-umami simultaneously. A royal Thai appetizer with ancient roots.

desserts.name: Tub Tim Grob (Crispy Rubies)
instructions: Tub tim grob is the Thai dessert of coated water chestnuts in sweet coconut milk
Tub tim = ruby; grob = crispy -- the name describes the red-coated, crispy-coated chestnuts
Water chestnuts are coated in tapioca flour then boiled -- the coating becomes translucent and chewy outside while the chestnut remains crunchy inside
Red coloring makes them ruby-like
Served in cold, lightly sweetened and salted coconut milk over ice
The contrast: chewy-crunchy tub tim against the cold coconut milk
desserts.description: Thai crispy rubies dessert -- water chestnut cubes coated in tapioca flour and colored red, boiled until the coating is translucent and chewy (the chestnut stays crunchy inside), served in cold sweetened-salted coconut milk over ice. Tub tim = ruby, grob = crispy: the name describes the texture.

desserts.name: Khanom Tako (Coconut Pudding Cups)
ingredients: Flour and arrowroot (for the base layer -- savory)
Water chestnuts or young coconut (for the base layer)
Thick coconut milk (for the sweet white top layer)
Pandan leaves (for flavoring and green color of the base)
instructions: Khanom tako are the two-layered Thai pudding cups
Served in small cups traditionally made from pandanus leaves (now often plastic or ceramic)
Two layers: a green-pandan savory-starchy base layer, and a white sweet-salty coconut milk top layer
The two layers stay separate -- the visual and textural contrast is the point
The top layer: thick coconut milk, slightly salted -- the salt enhances the sweetness
The base: may contain young coconut pieces or water chestnuts
The salt-sweet combination of coconut milk is a distinctly Thai-Southeast Asian dessert note
desserts.description: Thai two-layer coconut pudding cups -- a green pandan starchy base (savory-starchy) topped with sweet-salted thick coconut milk, served in small pandanus-woven cups. The two layers stay separate. The salted coconut milk layer is the Thai dessert signature -- salt enhancing the sweetness.

desserts.name: Bua Loi (Sticky Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
ingredients: Sesame (black and white) or pumpkin (for colored balls)
instructions: Bua loi are the Thai floating sticky rice balls
Small balls of glutinous rice flour dough -- colored with pandan, sesame, or natural colors
Boiled until they float -- floating means cooked
Served in warm, sweetened, lightly salted coconut milk
Eaten warm: the sticky, chewy rice balls in the fragrant coconut milk
The name: bua = lotus, loi = float -- floating lotus flowers
desserts.description: Thai floating sticky rice balls -- small glutinous rice flour balls colored with pandan (green) or sesame (gray), boiled until they float, served in warm sweetened-salted coconut milk. Bua loi means floating lotus. Chewy-sticky against the fragrant coconut milk.

drinks.name: Cha Yen (Thai Iced Tea)
ingredients: Thai tea blend (strong black tea with orange blossom water and food coloring)
instructions: Cha yen is the Thai iced tea -- one of the most recognizable Thai street drinks
Thai tea blend: a coarse black tea often with orange blossom water, vanilla, and red-orange food coloring
The tea is brewed very strong -- then chilled
Sweetened with condensed milk -- the thick, sweet base
Evaporated milk poured over the ice and tea -- it cascades down in a visual swirl
The deep amber tea with the white milk swirling: the iconic visual
Drunk through a straw to mix as you drink
drinks.description: Thai iced milk tea -- strong Thai tea blend (orange-red colored, often with orange blossom water) poured over ice, sweetened with condensed milk, evaporated milk poured over in a visual swirl. The amber-and-white visual is iconic. Drunk through a straw from every Thai street stall and restaurant.

drinks.name: Nam Manao (Thai Lime Soda)
ingredients: Sugar syrup or salt (Thai-style: a pinch of salt, not sugar, to balance)
instructions: Nam manao is the Thai fresh lime drink -- simple and essential
Fresh limes squeezed over ice and topped with soda water
The Thai version: often served with small sachets of sugar AND salt separately
Adding a pinch of salt to a sour-sweet drink is the Thai-Southeast Asian flavor habit -- the salt rounds the sourness
Much more sour and fresher than Western-style lemonade
drinks.description: Thai fresh lime soda -- squeezed lime juice over ice with soda water. The Thai way: served with sugar and a pinch of salt (the salt rounds the sourness: a Southeast Asian flavor habit). Much more sour than lemonade. Drunk at every Thai restaurant as the essential non-sweet refresher.

drinks.name: O Liang (Thai Iced Coffee)
ingredients: Thai coffee blend (coarse ground, often corn and other grains mixed in)
Hot water (brewed through a cloth filter bag)
Optional: black (no milk) is o liang; with milk is kafae yen
instructions: O liang is the Thai iced black coffee -- Chinese-influenced (Hokkien: black cool)
Brewed through a sock-like cloth filter bag (similar to Vietnamese phin drip method)
The coffee blend often includes roasted corn, chicory, and soybeans -- not pure coffee
Very strong and dark
Drunk black over ice -- no sugar, no milk
With condensed and evaporated milk it becomes kafae yen (Thai iced coffee with milk)
The cloth filter drip: the old Bangkok coffee shop method
drinks.description: Thai iced coffee -- o liang, brewed through a cloth filter bag from a Thai coffee blend (often mixed with roasted corn and chicory), poured over ice. Black: o liang (Hokkien Chinese for black cool). With condensed and evaporated milk: kafae yen. Chinese-Hokkien origin embedded in the old Bangkok kopitiam (coffee shop) culture.
